item.title: Low levels of common vitamin could be stealing nearly 30 minutes of your sleep
item.description: Low vitamin D blood levels were linked to about 23 minutes less sleep per night in a new study of adults 40 and older that used wearable sensors.
item.content:encoded:
Middle-aged and older adults with low levels of vitamin D slept about 23 minutes less per night than people with normal levels, according to a new study that tracked sleep with wearable sensors.

The study, led by the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health and the National Institute on Aging, used data collected from 2012 to 2019 as part of the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging.

The researchers looked at blood tests and sleep data from 460 adults ages 40 and older, averaging 71 years of age.

ONE TYPE OF SLEEP LINKED TO DRAMATICALLY LOWER RISK OF DEMENTIA, PARKINSON'S AND 81 OTHER DISEASES

After dividing the participants into three groups by vitamin D level, they found that the highest group slept nearly 20 minutes longer each night than the group with the lowest levels.

People with lower levels also stayed awake longer after waking up at night — a pattern that held regardless of age, gender or race.

The connection between vitamin D and sleep was strongest among Black participants, who made up about 22% of the group.

"Black adults in the United States have a higher prevalence of vitamin D deficiency and sleep disturbances compared to White adults, and may benefit more from increasing vitamin D levels," lead author Diefei Chen, a doctoral candidate in epidemiology at the Bloomberg School, said in a press release.

CAN WEARABLES DETECT HEART PROBLEMS EARLY? DOCTOR BREAKS DOWN REAL DATA

Most earlier studies on vitamin D and sleep relied on people reporting how well they thought they slept. In this study, researchers used blood draws and actigraphs, which are watch-like motion sensors that measure sleep and wake times.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The team also checked vitamin B12, which previous studies linked to sleep. While higher levels correlated with less nighttime wakefulness in women and more in men, the authors noted the results were statistically inconclusive.

The findings were published on Oct. 14 in The Journal of Gerontology: Medical Sciences.

Poor sleep and vitamin D deficiency are both widespread among older adults, with previous research linking sleep disturbances to higher risks of dementia, heart disease and diabetes.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The study had several limitations. Because the researchers looked at snapshots of data rather than testing a treatment in a clinical trial, they could only establish a link between vitamin D and sleep.

The findings did not prove that low levels cause poor sleep or that taking supplements will fix it.

Because blood tests can't distinguish between vitamin D from sunlight, food or supplements, the study could not determine whether the source matters.

In addition, the researchers did not track whether changing a person's vitamin D levels over several years leads to changes in their sleep.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Because everyone in the study was 40 or older and had no cognitive impairment, the results may not apply to younger people or adults with memory and thinking problems.

"These findings suggest that we should investigate more thoroughly whether boosting vitamin D levels can improve sleep health," senior author Adam Spira, a mental health professor at the Bloomberg School, said in the news release.

item.title: Eagles kicker didn't get ex-NFLer's memo about not digging into post-game Thanksgiving food
item.description: Derek Carr shares the cold Thanksgiving turkey warning that Eagles hero Jake Elliott apparently missed after his 59-yard field goal beat the Cowboys.
item.content:encoded:
Thanksgiving is a day for cramming absurd amounts of food into your mouth hole — and giving thanks, I suppose — but one ex-NFLer has a pro tip about when to show a little restraint.

And it would seem that Eagles' Thanksgiving hero Jake Elliott missed the memo.

Back in 2021, Derek Carr also led his team — the Las Vegas Raiders at the time — to a Thanksgiving win over the Dallas Cowboys.

COWBOYS LEGEND RANDY WHITE REVEALS INTENSE ENCOUNTER BETWEEN HIS MOTHER AND EAGLES FANS DURING PLAYING CAREER

As is tradition, he got to help himself to some of the broadcast's Turkey Day grub along with that game's hero, kicker Daniel Carlson.

"I have to share this every year," Carr said on his podcast "Home Grown with David & Derek Carr," per Daily Mail.

"So we're up there, we do the interview... and obviously Daniel made his kick. We're like: 'Daniel, you're going to eat the turkey.'"

Of course, few things top a good Thanksgiving meal, but we usually mean one that came straight out of the oven.

"It's definitely cold... [but] he goes to take a bite, and he says: 'Oh, delicious!'" Carr recalled. "And right as we walk away, I said, 'How was it?' He said: 'It was the grossest thing I've ever tasted.'"

It makes sense, especially for a game that goes down to the wire, that the food was prepped well in advance.

Of course, that also means it's not in its optimal eating window.

GIANTS STAR CAM SKATTEBO REVEALS THE ODD PREGAME MEAL THAT CAUSED TO HIM TO PUKE MID-GAME

Well, Elliott must not be subscribed to Carr's podcast because after sealing the Eagles' historic 39-38 comeback win with a 59-yard field goal, he dug right in.

Hey, the taste of sweet, sweet victory goes nicely with food that was probably intended just to be set dressing.

But, lest you think that Elliott had to do his Black Friday shopping while lying on the floor of his bathroom between bouts with food poisoning, think again.

The Eagles' hero was right back at it, getting fans fired up before the Philadelphia Flyers' Black Friday game against the Vancouver Canucks.

Looks like he fared better than most of us did on Thanksgiving, even though our food was much fresher than some stuffing warmed by studio lights.

item.title: NBC pulls controversial anti-Israel ad after igniting fury from Jewish groups
item.description: NBC pulled a controversial anti-Israel ad that aired during a primetime "Saturday Night Live" Thanksgiving special, sparking backlash among Jewish groups.
item.content:encoded:
NBC has pulled a controversial anti-Israel ad from its airwaves after sparking backlash over the Thanksgiving holiday, Fox News Digital has confirmed.

During a Thanksgiving-themed "Saturday Night Live" primetime special Wednesday night, NBC aired an ad featuring a girl raising money for a $400 bike, juxtaposing her with a Palestinian girl with a missing leg standing on crutches in front of a pile of rubble.

"Every three seconds, our government sends $400 of taxpayer money to Israel to do this," a narrator tells viewers while showing the injured Gazan child on screen.

MS RACHEL CALLS SILENCE ON GAZA CONFLICT 'F---ED UP,' SAYS IT UPSETS HER SO MUCH SHE NOW SWEARS

The 30-second ad, funded by the IMEU (Institute for Middle East Understanding) Policy Project, directs viewers to a website named No More For Israel, criticizing what it describes as the U.S. government's weapons "giveaway" to Israel and accusing the Jewish state of "committing a genocide" against Palestinians. The site urges Americans to pressure lawmakers to oppose any weapons deal with Israel.

Jewish groups and pro-Israel advocates criticized the ad as antisemitic, with many pointing out that the ad makes no mention that the ongoing conflict in Gaza began with the Oct. 7 terrorist attack committed by Hamas against Israel.

MANDANI GRILLED ON RHETORIC TOWARD OCT 7, COMBATTING ANTISEMITISM AS JEWISH NEW YORKERS FEAR CURRENT CLIMATE

"NBC took money to tell millions of Americans that our support for Israel is responsible for the horrific injury of a Palestinian child," American Jewish Committee CEO Ted Deutch wrote on X. 

"Here’s what the ad leaves out: the vicious Hamas terrorists who launched this war on October 7 by slaughtering, raping, and kidnapping Israelis, dragging hostages into Gaza, and then fighting from among Palestinian civilians, with horrific consequences for Israelis and Gazans alike.

"The suffering of Palestinian civilians is real and heartbreaking. But using that suffering to demonize Israel while writing Hamas out of the story isn’t an honest debate," the former Democratic congressman continued. 

"We can debate American policy and assistance to Israel. And yes, this was a paid advertisement. But 'we were paid to run it' cannot be the end of the discussion. Networks decide what they will and will not put on the air every day. NBC chose to take the money and run this ad.

"It should explain why and how an ad this one-sided and manipulative met its standards for what it will put on the air. And if this meets NBC’s standards, Americans deserve to know what those standards are."

The Israeli-American Council (IAC) characterized the ad as a clear example of "antisemitic blood libel aimed at denying the Jewish state its right to defend itself against terrorists and murderers."

"Words and images have consequences," the group shared in a statement to Fox News Digital. "They can normalize antisemitic hatred, embolden people to act on it and endanger innocent lives." 

The IAC called on NBC to "come clean about how this advertisement met its own standards and ensure it is not aired again." 

Anti-Defamation League CEO Jonathan Greenblatt also slammed NBC's decision to air the ad.

"Broadcasting an ad that blatantly demonizes the Jewish state and makes false claims about the use of American taxpayer dollars during primetime on the eve of a family holiday isn’t just insensitive. It’s indefensible," he wrote. 

"At a moment of escalating antisemitism, there is no rationale to justify fanning the flames with such a twisted narrative."

UK ANTISEMITISM ADVISOR LAUNCHES PROBE INTO BBC, SAYS CULTURE DEMANDS JEWISH STAFFERS 'JUSTIFY' EXISTENCE

"Modern day Nazi propaganda compliments of NBC. Every person who approved this ad buy should be identified and terminated," the advocacy group Stop Antisemitism wrote.

A source familiar with the matter told Fox News Digital that senior leadership at NBC was unaware of the ad until after it aired and that the network intends to reevaluate its ad review process going forward. The Wall Street Journal's Joe Flint first reported NBC's decision.

A spokesperson for NBC declined to comment.

item.title: Eagles running back compares heated argument with coach on sideline to arguing politics at Thanksgiving
item.description: Philadelphia Eagles running back Will Shipley likened his sideline argument with head coach Nick Sirianni to arguing politics at Thanksgiving.
item.content:encoded:
In case you were wondering what arguments are like on an NFL sideline, Philadelphia Eagles running back Will Shipley peeled back the curtain for you: It's like arguing politics at Thanksgiving.

After the Eagles were stopped by the Dallas Cowboys in the first half of their thrilling 39-38 win on Thursday at AT&T Stadium, Shipley and head coach Nick Sirianni got into an argument on the sideline.

"Emotions were running high," Shipley told reporters after the game. "Like on Thanksgiving, all families are arguing about politics and the drunk uncle."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"I've got so much love for Coach Nick and him as the leader of this football team."

Shipley said the two talked about it later when cooler heads prevailed and said there is no hard feelings between him and his head coach. The 24-year-old running back said Sirianni's passionate coaching style resonates with him.

"I mean, it really resonates with me because I wear my emotions on my sleeve as well. I have throughout my whole career and so for me to be able to just see him lead us in that way. It really resonates with me and I think resonates with everybody in this locker room," Shipley said.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Eagles star left tackle Jordan Mailata confirmed that Shipley and Sirianni were on good terms.

"They were loving each other up (in the locker room)," Mailata said, according to ESPN. "I was like, 'Oh, how come I'm not getting hugged like that?'"

Star running back Saquon Barkley went down with an injury early in the game, and Shipley was pressed into action. He ended up carrying the ball 10 times for 46 yards in the win. In seven games this season, Shipley has 34 carries for 112 yards with one touchdown.

The Eagles improved to 4-7 with the win and will look to carry the momentum from their two-game winning streak when they play the Arizona Cardinals next week.

item.title: From turkey shortages to helicopter deliveries: The extraordinary history of Thanksgiving during war
item.description: The U.S. military has delivered Thanksgiving dinner to troops from Civil War Union troops to Vietnam's War Zone D, a tradition born in wartime.
item.content:encoded:
In November 1966, 12 American soldiers stationed at an isolated outpost in a Vietnamese war zone were about as far from a traditional Thanksgiving at home as they could get.

Their only means of resupply was by air. But the U.S. military was determined to get them Thanksgiving dinner anyway.

A mess sergeant at Bien Hoa prepared turkey and all the trimmings, packed the meal into insulated containers and sent it by helicopter into War Zone D, where three officers and nine enlisted men of a 5th Special Forces detachment sat down to Thanksgiving dinner, according to Defense Department records preserved by the National Archives.

The delivery was one piece of a massive logistical effort the U.S. military has undertaken during wars spanning generations to get traditional Thanksgiving meals to troops serving in combat zones.

From civilians sending tens of thousands of turkeys to Union troops during the Civil War to helicopters carrying hot meals to soldiers in Korea, the holiday has been observed through some of the nation's most consequential conflicts.

Thanksgiving became a national tradition in the midst of war. President Abraham Lincoln issued his 1863 Thanksgiving proclamation as the Civil War entered its third year, calling on Americans to observe the final Thursday of November as a day of "Thanksgiving and Praise."

By the following year, Americans on the home front were mounting a massive effort to get Thanksgiving dinner to Union troops.

Former War Department official Charles A. Dana later recalled the "great turkey movement" of November 1864. In New York alone, organizers reported having 20,000 turkeys ready to send to the front, according to Dana's account. A Philadelphia committee sought transportation for another 4,000 destined for troops serving under Gen. Philip Sheridan.

By World War II, the effort to put turkey on troops' Thanksgiving tables had grown so large that it affected whether Americans at home could find one for their own.

In August 1943, the War Food Administration restricted most civilian turkey sales as the government sought millions of pounds for the armed forces. An initial goal of at least 10 million pounds for troops overseas was expanded to include military installations at home, and the government ultimately obtained roughly 30 million pounds before the order was lifted in October, according to wartime government records.

A year later, delivering Thanksgiving dinner near the front could carry its own risks.

102-YEAR-OLD NAVY VETERAN STILL CRAVES HOT WINGS AFTER 102 COMBAT MISSIONS IN KOREA: 'I MIGHT MAKE IT TO 115'

In Germany's Hürtgen Forest, Lt. Paul Boesch of the 121st Infantry Regiment later recalled being told that hot turkey dinners had arrived for his men amid some of the European campaign's most grueling fighting. Boesch protested that sending soldiers to collect the food would expose them to German artillery, but the order to distribute the meal stood.

His fears proved well-founded. As troops gathered to retrieve the food, German artillery struck the area, killing and wounding several men, according to Boesch's account.

Six years later, American troops were again eating Thanksgiving dinner near the front, this time in the bitter cold of North Korea.

On Thanksgiving Day 1950, Marines around the Chosin Reservoir were served turkey and cranberry sauce, candied sweet potatoes, fruitcake and mince pie. In the subzero temperatures, the food quickly began to freeze.

US NAVY RELEASES PHOTOS OF 'FRESH MEALS,' PUSHES BACK ON REPORTS OF FOOD SHORTAGES ON MIDDLE EAST WARSHIPS

The dinner came as U.S. commanders remained optimistic that the war could soon be over. The following day, Gen. Douglas MacArthur launched an offensive that became known as the "Home-by-Christmas" campaign.

Instead, Chinese forces entered the fighting in massive numbers. Within days of Thanksgiving, Marines around Chosin were surrounded and battling through one of the most brutal engagements of the Korean War.

More than half a century later, another generation of American troops was spending Thanksgiving at war in Iraq and Afghanistan.

In 2003, President George W. Bush secretly flew into Baghdad to surprise roughly 600 troops gathered for Thanksgiving dinner at Baghdad International Airport. Air Force One approached with its cabin shades drawn and lights dimmed amid tight security surrounding the trip.

"I was just looking for a warm meal somewhere," Bush joked before addressing the troops and helping serve Thanksgiving dinner.

In Afghanistan, getting that dinner to troops stationed far from major bases could require a different kind of operation.

On Thanksgiving 2007, helicopters carried turkeys and traditional fixings from Bagram Airfield to soldiers at remote firebases in the Tagab Valley, according to a contemporaneous U.S. military account.

It was the first hot meal some of the soldiers had eaten in months. Because the positions still had to be defended, troops rotated between Thanksgiving dinner and standing watch.

"The white meat was magnificent," Pfc. Matt Lorimer of the 82nd Airborne Division said.

At another remote Afghan outpost two years later, troops spent a month fattening five scrawny turkeys purchased locally for Thanksgiving. But five birds were not enough to feed roughly 150 soldiers.

Additional turkey was flown from the United States to Bagram Airfield and then transported to the outpost. Even that was not the end of the journey.

A handful of soldiers were manning an observation post on a mountain spur roughly 6,900 feet above sea level. Their Thanksgiving dinner was packed up and flown by helicopter up the mountain to them.

item.title: Steelers and Broncos players sending Aaron Rodgers signs through their scoring play celebrations
item.description: DK Metcalf held up eight fingers after scoring for the Steelers, while Broncos linebacker Alex Singleton imitated Aaron Rodgers "Discount Double Check."
item.content:encoded:
After much was made of Aaron Rodgers and the Pittsburgh Steelers this week, an actual game began between the quarterback's former team and the Denver Broncos on Friday.

And players from both teams made their scores about, you guessed it, Aaron Rodgers.

The Steelers took a surprising 14-0 lead in the first quarter, with the second of their scores coming on a 22-yard pass from new starting quarterback Mason Rudolph to DK Metcalf.

AARON RODGERS AND MIKE MCCARTHY DISAGREEMENTS AT HEART OF QUARTERBACK'S BENCHING BY THE STEELERS

And after the score, Metcalf made a couple of hand signals as his celebration. One of those was Metcalf holding up four fingers on each hand.

As in 8.

That was Rodgers' number in Pittsburgh.

Several people on social media who apparently read sign language translated Metcalf's sign language to mean: "Stand on business, 8."

In the second quarter, the Broncos scored their first points of the game when Alex Singleton tackled Jaylen Warren in the end zone for a safety.

And immediately Singleton started celebrating with an old-school Rodgers "Discount Double Check" celebration from maybe 15 years ago.

Pretty funny all around.

MIKE TOMLIN CALLS STEELERS SITUATION FOLLOWING AARON RODGERS VS. MIKE MCCARTHY FEUD 'A DUMPSTER FIRE'

Rodgers is gone from the Steelers. He sealed his fate this week when he went scorched-earth on Steelers coach Mike McCarthy.

That has become the biggest story around the NFL this week. It's clear players in the Steelers locker room, such as Metcalf, are not going to soon forget their former leader.

The Steelers, by the way, scored another touchdown when Jalen Ramsey returned a Bo Nix interception for a touchdown. Amazon Prime cameras cut to the crowd and sideline reaction rather than focusing on Ramsey after the score, so we don't know if he signaled on behalf of Rodgers, but it didn't seem so.

It is nonetheless wild that some Broncos players saw what happened Wednesday while they were on a short week of preparation, traveled across the country on Thanksgiving and still had time to come up with a celebration that spoke to the big story.

There's only one way to respond to this: Cheer for more reasons for celebration to see if Aaron Rodgers continues to haunt this game.

FOLLOW ARMANDO SALGUERO ON X: @ARMANDOSALGUERO

item.title: New California law could keep teens in booster seats until age 16 unless they pass test
item.description: Assemblymember Lori Wilson's seat belt fit test bill requires minors to pass five criteria before riding without a booster seat or in the front seat.
item.content:encoded:
Beginning in the new year, minors will be required to pass a five-step seat belt fit test before they can ride without a booster seat or sit in the front seat of a vehicle. The bill's author, Assemblymember Lori Wilson, cited figures showing that child injuries and fatalities in crashes have risen since the pandemic, with children ages 8 to 12 disproportionately affected.

"Extending the required age for booster use and implementing straightforward testing can significantly enhance child safety," CalMatters reported.

"So the best thing to do to keep your child safe while riding in a vehicle matches what our law is," Wilson said of the bill in April 2025. "It really is to take into consideration all the varying types of seats that we sit on in the car. This is about safety. 

"This is about making sure that if something happens, you are safe, and I think that’s the key thing that we’re trying to drive home is that it is not about treating people like babies."

3 CAR SEAT INSTALLATION MISTAKES YOU NEED TO AVOID

Previously, children ages 8 and older — or those at least 4 feet, 9 inches tall — could ride without a booster seat. Under the new law, Assembly Bill 435, children ages 8 to 15 may use a regular seat belt without a booster only if they meet all five criteria:

MELATONIN WARNINGS: NEARLY HALF OF PARENTS GIVE IT TO THEIR KIDS TO HELP THEM SLEEP, BUT EXPERTS URGE CAUTION

Improper car seat and booster use remains widespread, according to federal and industry studies.

GOT A TIP?

A 2011 National Child Restraint Use Special Study found that 46% of car seats and booster seats had at least one major installation or use error that could reduce their effectiveness in a crash.

Nearly all seats had some form of misuse, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration.

A 2021 study by AAA and the National Safety Council found that more than half of all car seats brought to child passenger safety technicians for inspection were improperly installed or used, and that only one in five parents and caregivers sought expert help securing their child's seat.

item.title: Liberal media and fans want Chiefs kicker Harrison Butker to fail because he's a Catholic conservative
item.description: Harrison Butker's critics, including Mina Kimes and Nick Wright, claim his activism has hurt his play, but his stats tell a more complicated story.
item.content:encoded:
Few NFL players have drawn as much personal disdain from the political left as Kansas City Chiefs kicker Harrison Butker.

The outspoken Catholic conservative has become a target for liberal sports fans and media personalities since delivering his 2024 commencement address at Benedictine College. His public support for Donald Trump, the Republican Party, campaigning with Senator Josh Hawley, and advocacy for traditional family values have only intensified that criticism.

Butker has been branded a misogynist for expressing the belief that motherhood is more fulfilling for women than climbing the corporate ladder. A stance that clearly aligns with his Catholic faith and those that attend Benedictine College, a Catholic college, which he was speaking too directly.

Since then, as we have seen from some of his most vocal critics, watching Butker miss field goals over the years, especially this season, appears to provide a sense of political vindication.

Unfortunately, the three-time Super Bowl champion has given those critics plenty of ammunition this season from media and fans.

WIFE OF PATRICK MAHOMES UNLEASHES FIRE AND FURY TOWARDS REFS AFTER BOTCHED CALL IN BUFFALO

Many media members are still taking shots at Butker for his comments in the commencement speech years later.

On Pablo Torre's Thanksgiving episode, he invited ESPN's Mina Kimes and the clip shared on X had a caption that said, "Harrison Butker may not like our Thanksgiving episode." The clip featured a male cook preparing some Thanksgiving dishes. Mina Kimes, still clearly triggered by Butker said, "How triggered do you think Harrison Butker would be if he turned this on and saw a bunch of men cooking for me?"

Good grief.

MINA KIMES CRACKS HARRISON BUTKER JOKE ABOUT MEN IN THE KITCHEN WITH CALLBACK TO KICKER'S COMMENCEMENT SPEECH

After the Chiefs worst game of the season on Sunday Night Football against the Seattle Seahawks, also being Butker's worst game of the season, going 1-for-3 on field goals, Nick Wright took a political shot at Butker.

"He started splitting his time between football and activism, and he hasn't been quite as good. That is just the timeline of it," Wright said.

There's clearly a political bias here and even making this topic political is unprofessional, in my opinion.

Also, Butker didn't immediately regress after becoming more politically outspoken. In fact, he converted every field goal and extra point he attempted between campaigning with Senator Josh Hawley during the Chiefs bye week in 2024 and suffering his knee injury. Maybe Wright should've spoken about how the knee injury and becoming the NFL's highest paid kicker could have effected Butker's performance.

On Thanksgiving fans took plenty of shots at Butker after missing a crucial 46-yard field goal with the game tied against the Buffalo Bills.

Denver news anchor Kyle Clark posted on X, "Butker. Wide right. Happy Thanksgiving, America." He later responded to a comment about rooting for and against players based on political party affiliation, Clark said, "Hi anonymous friend. Happy to clear this up for you. Whether my wife and my daughters should be able to have a job is not politics. It’s human rights. Have a Happy Thanksgiving!"

Again, a false retelling of what Butker said and believes.

Former Minnesota Star Tribune journalist Jim Souhan said, "Someone said that Butker’s pronouns are Miss/Misses and I’ll never forget it."

Editor-in Chief at radically liberal news outlet Meidas Touch, Ron Filipkowski took a shot as well by sharing a photo of Butker with President Trump on top of a post from an Associated Press reporter that stated, "Harrison Butker is tied with Trey Smack for most missed kicks this season with 9 (8 FGs, 1 PAT) and his 24 missed kicks (17 FGs, 7 PATs) since start of 2024 are most in NFL."

Obviously, when Butker misses to the right, the jokes write themselves, so those don't bother me. It's the low-hanging fruit that is easy to pick.

What we do need to discuss is how bad Butker has been statistically can be somewhat misleading.

In August 2024, 86 days after his controversial commencement speech at Benedictine College, the Kansas City Chiefs rewarded Butker with a four-year, $25.6 million contract extension, making him the highest-paid kicker in NFL history at the time. Whether you're right, left, or center, you could agree at that time, Butker deserved this. The Chiefs clearly did not care that liberals were calling for Butker to be cut from the team for his comments on traditional roles within the household.

Butker was coming off a 2023 campaign in which he converted 33 of his 35 field goal attempts and made every extra point. He also drilled a Super Bowl-record 57-yard field goal against the San Francisco 49ers. He was arguably the Super Bowl MVP for much of the game.

Unfortunately, his field goal percentage has declined every season since signing that lucrative extension.

Butker currently owns the worst field goal percentage among NFL kickers with at least 15 attempts this season. However, a closer examination of his numbers reveals that his struggles are overwhelmingly concentrated in one area: long-distance field goals.

According to NFL.com, Butker has converted just two of his eight attempts from 50-plus yards this season (25%). From inside 50 yards, he's 13-of-15 (86.7%), including a perfect 7-of-7 from inside 40 yards.

It's particulary shocking to see how bad he's been from distance because he hit a 69-yard field goal in preseason, which most likely would've been good from almost 80 yards.

HARRISON BUTKER'S 69-YARD FIELD GOAL DEMONSTRATES THE NFL'S LATEST BIG SCORING CONTROVERSY

Butker isn't the only highly compensated kicker struggling from deep, either.

Dallas Cowboys kicker Brandon Aubrey, who surpassed Butker as the highest-paid kicker in NFL history after signing a four-year, $28 million extension in April, is also experiencing the worst season of his career.

Aubrey has converted just six of his 11 attempts from 50-plus yards (54.5%) and is shooting a career-low 77.8% overall. He also missed a 40-yard field goal on Thanksgiving in Dallas' one-point loss to Philadelphia. That kick has been heavily debated online, with former Colts punter and placeholder Pat McAfee giving Aubrey grace because the laces were facing toward Aubrey.

Speaking about Aubrey's stats are not an excuse for Butker's poor performance, but it does provide some much-needed perspective. Clearly his struggles are not as scrutinized as Butker's, though he's paid more.

There is a difference between rooting for someone to fail because of their religious and political beliefs and legitimately criticizing their professional performance.

Butker deserves the latter right now.

If you know me at all, I am not a LeBron James fan. Yes, his politics come into play in my dislike of him, but claiming poor play is because of campaigning for Hilary Clinton or Kamala Harris by me would hopefully cause many to scold me for refusing to provide proper sports analysis and instead, going for a political cheapshot.

In all honestly, I'd love nothing more than to see Butker return to being one of the most reliable kickers in football. But defending his right to express his Catholic faith and conservative values doesn't require defending his inability to consistently put a football through the uprights, especially from long distance.

The Chiefs are paying him elite money to deliver elite results, particularly in high-pressure situations with championship aspirations on the line. He has no one to blame but himself. He needs to be better.

Butker doesn't need to apologize for his faith, his political affiliations or his appreciation for traditional family values. He just needs to start making kicks again.

Until he does that, his critics, in and out of the media, will continue to tee off on who they consider to be their political enemy.

item.title: Donald Trump Jr criticizes Netflix over racy 'Hunting Wives' Thanksgiving post
item.description: Donald Trump Jr. called out Netflix after the streamer posted a steamy "The Hunting Wives" clip on Thanksgiving, asking "What is wrong with you???"
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump Jr. publicly called out Netflix on Thursday after the streaming platform shared footage of a steamy lovemaking session to mark Thanksgiving Day.

Netflix’s official account on X promoted the latest season of its show, "The Hunting Wives," by sharing a racy bedroom scene with lead actresses Brittany Snow and Malin Åkerman. Alongside the footage, the streaming service wrote, "This thanksgiving plate."

Trump Jr. was one of many people who found the post to be in poor taste to mark a holiday where families share a meal together. He wrote on X, "What is wrong with you??? It’s Thanksgiving."

A LOOK AT HOW THE TRUMPS SPEND THEIR THANKSGIVING HOLIDAY THROUGH THE YEARS

The post racked up nearly 35 million views by Friday. 

On its official website, Netflix summarized that the series, "Based on the bestselling novel by May Cobb, The Hunting Wives follows a woman as she and her family move from Boston to Texas. There, she grows close to a socialite — maybe too close — and becomes consumed by obsession, seduction, and murder."

Fox News Digital reached out to film critic Christian Toto, host of the "Hollywood in Toto" podcast, about the controversy, one of many experienced by the platform.

"Companies should err on the side of caution when sharing social media posts. That's advice Netflix doesn't always heed. The streamer's latest blast, tied to the guilty pleasure ‘Hunting Wives,’ is a perfect example of digital tone deafness," he wrote.

HOW WOKE HOLLYWOOD IS REMAKING, AND RUINING, EVERY FILM YOU'VE EVER LOVED

"Netflix isn't a family-friendly company by any stretch, but that kind of social media post is very sexual and hardly fitting [for] a major corporation. There are a million ways to creatively showcase your content. Netflix ... chose poorly. And the timing was awful, to boot," he concluded.

Fox News Digital also reached out to Netflix and did not receive an immediate reply.

item.title: Cowboys' Jerry Jones makes statement on Brian Schottenheimer's future after embarrassing Thanksgiving loss
item.description: Jerry Jones said he doesn't anticipate any immediate coaching changes after the Dallas Cowboys' blown 21-10 lead against the Philadelphia Eagles.
item.content:encoded:
While Dallas Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer may have had a rough Thanksgiving after his team's embarrassing loss on Thursday, he will at least be thankful for keeping his job for another week.

Cowboys owner Jerry Jones said that despite blowing a 21-10 third-quarter lead in its 39-38 loss to the undermanned Philadelphia Eagles at AT&T Stadium, he doesn't anticipate making any coaching changes before the team's next game. However, the 84-year-old was asked what gives him confidence that Schottenheimer can still be a good head coach, and Jones didn't exactly give a ringing endorsement.

"Nothing you've seen out here tonight. You have to look at everything," Jones told reporters postgame. "You can and should look at every person that’s had a hand in this, and you should do that."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Despite the humiliating loss, Jones did say that he thinks Schottenheimer can lead the Cowboys to a Super Bowl.

"I do," he said. "But on the other hand, these are setbacks and they’re damning setbacks, there's no question about it, especially when we feel like that we can look at parts of the game where it was ours to take and we didn’t. When you look at every bit of it, then you have to question everything."

The Eagles started Joe Milton, who was on the Cowboys squad last month, at quarterback. The 26-year-old shredded the porous Cowboys defense in the second half, as he completed 21 of 31 passes for 331 yards with three touchdowns and one interception, along with 15 rushing yards and one touchdown.

During the Cowboys' collapse, they missed a 40-yard field goal that would have put them up two scores late in the fourth quarter and would have effectively sealed the game. They had a punt get blocked for a touchdown, breathing life back into the Eagles sideline at the beginning of the fourth quarter.

Jones said the entire organization is responsible for the loss.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"It’s a bitter disappointment to have done some things early that we did and turn around every phase, every phase, that’s a part of a game like this," Jones said. "All three teams, ownership, coaching, everybody is responsible for what we saw at the end of this game."

The loss dropped the Cowboys to 5-7 on the season and was devastating to their playoff hopes. Compounding issues for Dallas is they have a very difficult schedule to end the season.

Jones said the team is focused on their upcoming schedule and not any coaching changes. Already this season, the Cowboys have stripped defensive coordinator Christian Parker of play-calling duties and given them to Mike Pettine. However, the early returns haven't been positive.

Missing the playoffs would be a major disappointment for the Cowboys, as the rest of the NFC East has been ravaged by injuries and underperformance. The Giants lost Jaxson Dart to injury in Week 2, Eagles star quarterback Jalen Hurts is out for the season with blood clots and the Commanders have been ravaged by injuries to key players on both sides of the ball.

Yet, despite the Cowboys being largely healthy, they have yet to win back-to-back games this season and gain any traction in the NFC playoff race. If the Cowboys fizzle down the stretch, the heat on Schottenheimer's job will only intensify.

item.title: The Killers guitarist Dave Keuning went blind in one eye during life-threatening stroke
item.description: Dave Keuning says his wife's fast action got him into stroke surgery after a brain clot; the first thing he checked after waking was his guitar.
item.content:encoded:
The Killers guitarist Dave Keuning survived a major stroke after doctors gave him just a 40% chance to live.

Keuning, 50, opened up about the medical emergency on Thanksgiving, using the holiday to share both his recovery and the recent birth of his daughter, Odette.

"Three months ago, we had our baby girl, Odette," he shared on Instagram. "Two weeks ago, I had a major stroke, and thanks to my wife acting fast, I went straight to the hospital and into surgery."

COUNTRY SINGER DRAKE WHITE ADMITS HE STILL FEARS ANOTHER STROKE SEVEN YEARS AFTER NEARLY DYING

"The first hour after a stroke is critical when it comes to getting to the hospital. I had a blood clot in my brain that cut off the blood supply to the entire right side of my brain," Keuning explained. "By the time I arrived at the hospital, I was blind in one eye and had lost function on my left side, but I still wasn’t able to realize I was having a stroke."

Doctors warned Keuning he had only a 40% chance of survival and would face lasting disabilities, though the guitarist said he miraculously made a full recovery.

"And yes I can play guitar just as good as before," Keuning clarified. "It was the first thing I checked when I woke up from surgery."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Beyond his ability to return to music, Keuning said the experience left him grateful for his overall recovery and his loved ones.

"I feel extremely fortunate that I am alive and well, and that I can use my hands and feet and talk just like before," he said. "I am thankful for my wife, my son, my daughter, and all of my bandmates, who I feel closer to than ever."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Keuning began playing guitar in high school before relocating to Las Vegas in 2000. While working at a retail store on the Las Vegas Strip, he placed a classified ad in a local newspaper seeking musicians to form a rock band. Singer Brandon Flowers answered the ad, and the pair teamed up with bassist Mark Stoermer and drummer Ronnie Vannucci Jr. to launch The Killers in 2001.

The group took its name from a fictional band featured on a bass drum in the music video for New Order's song "Crystal."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

With the band, Keuning co-wrote and performed on their breakout hit "Mr. Brightside" plus their 2004 debut album "Hot Fuss." He is also featured on follow-ups "Sam's Town" along with "Day & Age."

Their biggest hit singles include "Mr. Brightside," "Somebody Told Me," "All These Things That I've Done," "When You Were Young," and "Human." Across their career, The Killers have released seven studio albums, all of which reached No. 1 on the UK Albums Chart.

After stepping back from touring in 2017, Keuning rejoined The Killers for their 2021 album "Pressure Machine."

item.title: Aaron Rodgers and Mike McCarthy's family members getting involved in public Steelers feud
item.description: Jordan Rodgers says Mike McCarthy's alleged meeting behavior is "unacceptable and unprecedented" and questions whether he stays Steelers head coach.
item.content:encoded:
Aaron Rodgers and Mike McCarthy’s bitter split in Pittsburgh has become a family affair on Thanksgiving weekend.

The quarterback’s brother questioning the coach’s future and the coach’s daughter sharing posts defending her father.

Jordan Rodgers criticized McCarthy during a Friday appearance on "Good Morning America," while Alex McCarthy used Instagram to amplify support for her dad following Aaron Rodgers’ public attack on his former coach.

MIKE MCCARTHY'S OLDEST DAUGHTER DEFENDS HER DAD AGAINST AARON RODGERS' NASTY ATTACKS

The dueling shows of family support followed Pittsburgh’s decision to release Rodgers on Wednesday, a day after benching him in favor of Mason Rudolph. Rodgers had accused McCarthy of missing meetings and falling asleep during others in an appearance on "The Pat McAfee Show."

Jordan described the alleged behavior as "unacceptable and unprecedented" and questioned whether McCarthy would remain in charge.

"I would be surprised if he continued to be the head coach moving forward," Jordan said Friday on Good Morning America.

"Having been in locker rooms, having been a third-string quarterback on a practice squad … if I even looked like I was nodding off, I’d be cut in a second," he said. "And to have that happen from the head coach, a play caller, you can’t play football that way and there’s too many jobs at stake for people to put up with that type of behavior."

"So I think the Steelers’ll look into this, but seemingly, the accusations and allegations are confirmed in a lot of ways and he didn’t refute them," Jordan said, adding that it was a "weird way to see it end."

Drawing on his own experience as a practice squad quarterback, Jordan argued that a player could lose his job for appearing to nod off in a meeting. He said a head coach and offensive play caller should face scrutiny when other people’s livelihoods are at stake.

FORMER NFL PLAYERS DEFEND AARON RODGERS AFTER STEELERS RELEASE HIM AMID MIKE MCCARTHY DISPUTE

His defense of Aaron comes after the brothers repaired their own fractured relationship. Aaron revealed in September that they had reconciled following years of estrangement, describing difficult conversations as part of reconnecting with his parents and siblings. He credited his wife, Brittani, with helping him reach that point.

Alex McCarthy, meanwhile, shared an Instagram story from singer John Vincent featuring a photograph of him embracing her father.

Vincent praised McCarthy as a Super Bowl-winning coach and "an even better human being," adding that he was proud to call him his brother.

Alex also shared on her Instagram story clips of NFL on FOX insider Jay Glazer and former Steelers quarterback Terry Bradshaw defending McCarthy. Bradshaw criticized Rodgers’ handling of his departure and suggested the quarterback had failed to show class.

Then, after the Cowboys lost to the Eagles on Thanksgiving, Alex posted a quote from Cowboys owner Jerry Jones defending McCarthy.

"I never had the type of thing that is being said about him," Jones said of McCarthy.

McCarthy addressed the rupture Wednesday, declining to detail private conversations with Rodgers while acknowledging a disagreement and an ultimatum. He said his players and coaches were focused on their next opponent, Denver.

"I know how to win," McCarthy said, "and that’s the facts."

Steelers president Art Rooney II backed McCarthy’s future and called Rodgers’ conduct insubordinate in a Thanksgiving interview with the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette.

Pittsburgh’s release announcement said Rodgers threw for 2,241 yards and 16 touchdowns in 10 starts this season. He initially joined the team in 2025 and re-signed in the offseason.

The breakup ends a reunion between a quarterback and coach who previously worked together in Green Bay from 2006 through 2018. Pittsburgh is turning to Rudolph for Friday’s game against the Broncos after entering the week 6-4 and still in playoff position.

item.title: The retro canned-soup recipe home cooks are pulling out for Thanksgiving leftovers
item.description: Campbell's 2026 State of the Sides report says 51% of Americans find the table incomplete without green bean casserole, a top side dish in Thanksgiving and leftover meals.
item.content:encoded:
Thanksgiving dinner and all the leftover-packed lunches and dinners that follow the big meal are usually incomplete without one staple side that was never even intended to be a fixture of the holiday weekend's celebrations.

Dorcas Reilly, a supervisor in Campbell’s test kitchen, developed a meal plan in 1955 that combined canned green beans and condensed cream of mushroom soup.

It came about because an Associated Press food editor asked Campbell’s for an easy vegetable side made with common pantry ingredients, according to Smithsonian Magazine. 

Reilly and her team tested additions such as ham and celery salt before settling on the simple combination that became Green Bean Bake.

THANKSGIVING SCRAPS REINVENTED BY TOP CHEFS FOR DELICIOUS, EASY-TO-MAKE MEALS

The dish originally included green beans, cream of mushroom soup, milk, soy sauce, black pepper and French-fried onions. 

It gained popularity after Campbell's printed it on soup cans.

Nearly 50 years later, in 2002, Reilly was inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame, and her handwritten recipe was donated to the museum.

Now, more than 70 years later, the casserole remains a staple of many Americans' Thanksgiving dinners. In Campbell’s 2026 State of the Sides report, 67% of respondents said it reminds them of Thanksgivings past, while 51% said the table would feel incomplete without it. 

YOUR FAVORITE GROCERY AND SNACK ITEMS MAY HAVE DISAPPEARED FROM STORE SHELVES IN 2026

Only 19% said they would change the recipe, the lowest share among the top five Thanksgiving sides, which include stuffing, mashed potatoes, yams and sweet potatoes and macaroni and cheese.

Campbell’s sells nearly 40 million cans of cream of mushroom soup during Thanksgiving month, accounting for about 30% of its annual sales of the soup, enough to make 40 million casseroles, the company told Fox News Digital.

Campbell’s says the nearly 40 million cans contain enough soup to fill the entire Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade balloon fleet.

RESTAURANTS BRING BACK OLD-SCHOOL HOSPITALITY AS NOSTALGIA TAKES HOLD ACROSS AMERICA

Over the past five holiday seasons, it sold more than 308 million cans.

"We’re proud that Campbell’s has been part of those traditions for generations, with trusted recipes that make holiday cooking a guaranteed success," Rebecca Duke, senior director of brand marketing at The Campbell’s Company, said in a statement.

CELEBRITY CHEF SAYS PEOPLE HAVE SOUTHERN FOOD ALL WRONG, SHARES WHAT HER FAMILY ATE

Green bean casserole has a particularly strong following in the Midwest, where it appears on 60% of Thanksgiving tables, according to the report.

Nebraska and Missouri lead the region, with 70% and 68% of respondents, respectively, serving it. 

More than half of Midwesterners, or 54%, called it the region’s most iconic side.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

While many people prefer serving the comforting and recognizable combination most guests are familiar with, some home cooks do add their own touches, Campbell's noted, from cheese and bacon to fresh mushrooms and herbs.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

Online, opinions vary about both the casserole itself and how it should be made.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Green bean casserole is a strangely polarizing dish," one person said in a Reddit discussion in r/Thanksgiving.

One fan said, "I only have it on Thanksgiving, but I love green bean casserole."

A detractor said, "I would be thrilled if someone had an alternative green bean dish."

Another Reddit commenter said, "I love green bean casserole if it’s made with fresh beans."

Yet another made the case for the traditional version in all its canned glory: "[The mushier] the better with canned green beans."

item.title: Nick Sirianni goes after fans in the stands after stunning comeback, amazing Rodgers stat & Kristin Cavallari!
item.description: Nick Sirianni unloaded on fans after the Eagles' stunning win in Dallas, and the fiery Black Friday moment has Philly wondering if his time is done.
item.content:encoded:
'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday-Friday on OutKick.com.

The Friday after Thanksgiving — yes, also known as Black Friday — always feels so weird to me.

Frankly, I went through most of yesterday thinking it was Sunday. It felt like a Sunday, didn't it? No work. Football. Drinking and eating all day. You passed out on the couch watching what looked and sounded like a Sunday Night Football game.

I woke up this morning and had that usual Monday morning feeling of dread. And then it hit me — it's not Monday. BUT, it's also not Saturday. I have to work today despite being off all day yesterday.

But, it's also a Friday ... and a holiday Friday, at that. There's football all day long. The Egg Bowl this afternoon. UF-FSU. And then, just when you think it's only college games ... BAM. We get a horrible Broncos-Steelers NFL game at 3.

So, is today a work day? Eh. Not really. It's one of those tweeners. We're working ... but are we really working?

Let's coast through this day together, and get this class GOING.

Welcome to a Friday Nightcaps — the one where Nick Sirianni took out all of his anger on the fans after yesterday's stunner in Dallas. Love him or hate him, you can't say Nick doesn't have the passion.

He's a psycho. You'll see.

What else? I've got Danny Kannell with a disgusting Thanksgiving hack, some solid fan mail on a holiday Friday, and an incredible stat about Aaron Rodgers that blew my mind.

How is this even possible? You'll see.

Grab you a discounted beverage on this Black Friday, and settle in for an end-of-the-week 'Cap!

Serious question ... did anyone camp outside a Best Buy at 3 a.m. this morning waiting to buy a giant TV for $150? I wrote about it a few weeks ago, but I think Black Friday has lost all of its luster.

The internet, of course, has completely killed it. Amazon, to be specific. Amazon runs "Black Friday" deals all month long. Sort of destroys this once-beautiful day, doesn't it? I haven't been inside an actual department store in years. We only have one — Dillard's — still open in our town.

HOW TO SPOT REAL BLACK FRIDAY SAVINGS THIS HOLIDAY SEASON AMID THE AFFORDABILITY SQUEEZE

The rest of the mall has been torn to shreds over the past six months. It's all gone ... except the Dillard's.

Wild. How did they pull THAT one off?

Anyway, let me know if you still ventured out this morning. I'm curious to see if anyone still does it.

Now, let's get this (short) class started with Nick Sirianni going AFTER fans yesterday after a stunning fourth quarter in Dallas:

EAGLES BENCH TANNER MCKEE FOR JOE MILTON TWO DAYS AFTER GIVING HIM VOTE OF CONFIDENCE: REPORT

Thoughts?

Obviously, Nick Sirianni is a firecracker. Always has been. I feel like Eagles fans are done with him, even though he won a Super Bowl a few years ago. Has he run his course in Philadelphia?

Perhaps Joe Milton will save his job. Seriously. Milton was amazing yesterday. The guy has the strongest arm I've ever seen out of a quarterback.

The NFC East is pretty open right now, even with the Giants winning Sunday. I'm not sure I'd count Philly out just yet, especially with Sirianni suddenly feeling himself again.

UPDATE: The internet seems to think Sirianni was chirping at an EAGLES fan who berated him after halftime. I'm not going to share the video because it's vulgar and I don't want to get fired on Black Friday, but feel free to watch it here and form your own opinion.

OK, let's leave one disgusting act and check in with another ...

This one comes courtesy of Danny Kannell, who stunned Twitter yesterday by admitting he douses his turkey in ...

Ketchup?

Be honest, folks — have you EVER put ketchup on a turkey? I'm the biggest ketchup fan in the world. I love the stuff. I'd eat it on just about anything.

But turkey? I've never even considered it. Not once. I'm not sure I've ever been at a Thanksgiving table with ketchup even an option.

Danny is getting crushed on Twitter for the behavior, but I'm not ready to pass judgment just yet. Maybe I'm missing something? I doubt it, but I'll let y'all tell me.

Zach.Dean@OutKick.com.

OK, let's rapid-fire this holiday class into a big weekend of FOOTBALL. First up? Is this the most insane stat of all time?

Aaron Rodgers and Patrick Mahomes have NEVER played each other? That seems impossible, but I looked it up, and it's true.

Amazing.

The woke AI bot on Google tells they've had three chances to play each other, but one was hurt/"sick" each time.

Three chances, and three whiffs. It's one of those obscure facts that sounds too insane to be true.

Also ... Patrick Mahomes has been in the league for 10 years? TEN years?

Lordy, we're getting old.

Next? Let's get to some fan mail on the way out!

From DJD:

"Saw your article about that bad call in the Kent State/Eastern Michigan game. You’re right it was a bad call, then you had to double down and disparage the city it was played in. What an arrogant a–hole! A lot of places to get news from. We don’t need you, Fox, or Outkick to survive. Come back when you grow up."

Thanks, DJD! For those who missed it, earlier this week I wrote about Kent State getting absolutely jobbed in Tuesday's loss to Eastern Michigan after the refs reversed a walk-off touchdown.

Eastern Michigan is located in Ypsilanti, Michigan — a place I admittedly had never heard of until Wednesday.

Here's the line that sent DJD into a tailspin:

"Sure, you didn't know that was an actual place until right now, but I promise you, it is."

That's it! As someone who grew up next to a town called "Yeehaw Junction" I can assure you, DJD, I meant no disrespect to the fine folks of Ypsilanti.

OK, that's it for today — and this week!

On the way out, here's Kristin Cavallari with a humdinger of a Black Friday sale.

See y'all Monday.

item.title: Seattle bar owner refuses to back down after declaring 'Ladies' Night' is for 'biological women' only
item.description: Art Marble 21 owner Danny Pentin stands by his Ladies' Night discount policy as the Seattle Office for Civil Rights reviews two complaints over the email.
item.content:encoded:
A Seattle bar owner is standing by his beliefs about biological sex after a leaked email outlining who should receive Ladies' Night discounts ignited controversy — insisting his establishment welcomes transgender customers and has never discriminated against anyone.

"Ladies night is for women. Biological women," Danny Pentin, owner of Art Marble 21, said in an email shared with FOX 13.

The local Seattle outlet reported that the email also stated that, "Men dressed in women's clothing are not women, nor are they ladies," and also included that, "If they have a mustache, or can grow one, the ladies night promo does not apply to them. If they have an Adam's apple, not applicable."

SAN FRANCISCO YMCA CHANGES LOCKER ROOM RULES AFTER TRANSGENDER CONTROVERSY: REPORT

Pentin also wrote, "There has to be a place in Seattle that defers to common sense and biology before ideology and politics and we are that place."

Pentin, however, told FOX 13 that he is not against those who are going through gender confusion.

"No, I'm not anti people. I mean, I love everybody for where they're at, right," Pentin said. "If people who go through dealing with body dysmorphia and those things, those are real things that people have to deal with."

According to an Instagram statement from Pentin, the controversy began in late August when a bartender was allegedly assaulted by a customer following a dispute over eligibility for a discounted drink during Ladies' Night.

MASSACHUSETTS LESBIAN BAR IGNITES FURY AFTER EASING MASK RULES FOR ONE NIGHT A WEEK

Pentin said the bar initially had no formal restrictions on who could receive the discounts, leaving those decisions to individual bartenders. 

Following the alleged incident, he sent an internal email on Sept. 19, speaking to what he described as customers exploiting a promotion intended for women. Pentin said the email remained private until Nov. 17, when a former bartender leaked it publicly, sparking backlash over his views on biological sex and the bar's discount policy.

In his public response, Pentin defended his personal beliefs while insisting that Art Marble 21 has never discriminated against customers or prohibited transgender individuals from entering the establishment.

NEW HAMPSHIRE WOMAN SAYS PLANET FITNESS CANCELED HER MEMBERSHIP AFTER SHE REPORTED MAN IN LOCKER ROOM

He emphasized that the views expressed in the email were his alone and did not necessarily reflect those of his employees.

"On its face the leaked email appears to suggest we do not allow trans people into our establishment," Pentin wrote in the Instagram statement. "That is simply not true. If we did not allow trans people into our establishment, it would have been made known long before this email was taken out of context. My personal stance is made known in the email, but it does not reflect the beliefs of the employees that work at Art Marble 21. These are my beliefs and mine alone. We respect each other's beliefs. My staff would not work for me for years if they believed I was a bigot, a racist or any of the other buzz words used to condemn people who think differently than those who have made this into what it has become."

He said he respects people's freedom to live according to their own beliefs and expects that respect to be reciprocated. Pentin concluded by reaffirming his convictions and insisting that Art Marble 21 remains a welcoming establishment, saying it has never been discriminatory and never will be.

In a statement to Fox News Digital, a spokesperson for the Seattle Office of Civil Rights said that gender and gender identity are protected classes under Seattle’s Public Accommodations Ordinance that prohibits discriminatory practices, and that businesses cannot legally deny a promotional discount based on a customer's sex, gender identity, or gender expression.

FEMALE VIRGINIA OFFICER SUES POLICE DEPARTMENT AFTER ALLEGEDLY SHARING LOCKER ROOM WITH BIOLOGICAL MALE

The Seattle Office for Civil Rights said they received two complaints regarding Art Marble 21's "Ladies' Night" promotion, one on Nov. 17 and one on Nov.19, and are "following up with the individuals who submitted the complaints to determine if they qualify to file a claim and whether they wish to proceed with that process."

Fox News Digital reached out to Pentin for comment but did not immediately hear back.
